source: Numina & Kimi Team (2025) Kimina-Prover Preview (arXiv v1, 15 Apr 2025)
finding: The four numbers 52.94, 68.85, 77.87 and 80.74 are Kimina-Prover Preview (72B) results on miniF2F-test. They are the Kimina paper's own table, at pass@1, 32, 1024 and 8192.
numbers: Kimina-Prover Preview 72B, miniF2F-test: pass@1 52.94%, pass@8 65.16%, pass@32 68.85%, pass@1024 77.87%, pass@8192 80.74%. Distilled 1.5B: 42.6%. Subsets at pass@8192: IMO 40.00%, AIME 86.67%.
quote: With just pass@1, the model already achieves 52.94%, and with pass@32, it reaches 68.85%
limits: Lab self-report. Kimina used a revised miniF2F. Pass@8192 uses a very large sample budget.
agent_relevance: Closes the clash in claim K10/b19: cite these as Kimina numbers, not DeepSeek.

source: Ren et al. (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2, Table 1 and Table 3
finding: DeepSeek-Prover-V2's Table 1 copies Kimina's four numbers into the Kimina row. DeepSeek's own rows are different and higher. Text extraction of the layout mixes the rows, which is how the numbers got attributed to both.
limits: Table 1 compares pass@k at different sample budgets and different Lean/miniF2F revisions. Kimina's own revision differs.
agent_relevance: Resolved: DeepSeek V2 does not hold 52.94/68.85/77.87/80.74. K10 and K13 should cite 61.9/82.4/86.6/88.9 for V2.

source: Ren et al. (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2, Table 3 token counts, plus our arithmetic
finding: Reasoning mode (CoT with subgoal decomposition) writes 9-15 times more tokens per sample than non-CoT, yet wins when we match total tokens. This is a derived comparison, not run by the authors.
numbers: Tokens per sample on miniF2F-test: 7B non-CoT 442.6, CoT 4488.5; 671B non-CoT 761.8, CoT 6751.9. Derived totals: 671B non-CoT pass@1024 = 1024*761.8 = 780k tokens for 76.7%; 671B CoT pass@32 = 32*6751.9 = 216k tokens for 82.4%. 7B: non-CoT pass@1024 about 453k tokens for 73.2% vs CoT pass@32 about 144k tokens for 75.6%.
limits: The two modes are two prompts of one model trained with a cold start built from decomposition. It is not a flat-vs-decomposed ablation on the same model. Unit is output tokens only (no prompt tokens). Averages over samples, not over solved problems.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 7: reasoning plus decomposition wins at 3.6x fewer output tokens in this one pair. It is still not a clean test of lemma decomposition alone.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Equal-budget test of verify-and-repair against plain resampling, with unit tests as the checker (code, not proofs). Gains are small, sometimes negative, and best when the budget goes to fresh samples, not to repair.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each (up to 20 samples) gives 1.05x the pass rate of pass@20; 2 initial samples plus 10 repairs each (22 samples) gives 0.97x of pass@22. Code Llama 13B gains up to 10% over baseline with GPT-4 feedback; GPT-3.5 gains up to 3%. Models: Code Llama-13b-instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; HumanEval and APPS.
quote: self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on its own code
limits: Python tasks with unit tests. Budget measured as tokens (pass@t). Feedback quality is the bottleneck. Repair success and resampling success rise together with task ease.
agent_relevance: Strongest equal-compute evidence: do not assume repair beats resampling. Spend most budget on diverse first attempts, a few on repair; use a stronger or external checker for feedback.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet, human-feedback study
finding: When an expert human gives the debugging explanation, GPT-4 repair improves much. So the weak step is the model's own diagnosis, not the rewriting.
numbers: Fraction of repaired programs that pass: 33.3% with GPT-4's own feedback vs 52.6% with expert human feedback (1.58x). Small-scale study.
limits: Small human study (few programmers, few problems). Not a proof-assistant setting.
agent_relevance: For S8: an external checker message is worth more than a self-critique. Prefer executable error text; if only self-critique exists, expect little gain.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2 (verifier-guided self-correction)
finding: Compiler-guided revision gives about +2 points at pass@32/64 on miniF2F and +14 PutnamBench solves. Removing the compiler error text hurts. A 32-sample run with 5 revision rounds beats the no-correction model at 8192 samples.
numbers: 32B: miniF2F pass@32 88.1% to 90.4% with correction; 92.7% at pass@32 with 128k context and 5 rounds vs 92.2% at pass@8192 without correction. PutnamBench 86 solved at pass@184 (57 at pass@32). Setup: first round 30k tokens, 2 rounds, 40k total tokens in correction mode. Removing error messages lowers accuracy; removing previous CoT lowers it slightly.
limits: Same lab, trained a model for this (correction data in SFT and RL). The 32 vs 8192 comparison is not token matched in the paper. Our arithmetic: up to 32*128k = 4.1M vs 8192*30k = 246M tokens, so correction wins at under 2% of the tokens. Concurrent Seed-Prover footnote: its test budget is unknown.
agent_relevance: Supports K04 for trained provers: checker text in context helps at low cost. A prompt-only agent has no such training; treat as upper bound.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Seed-Prover (ByteDance Seed)
finding: Light inference is refine-with-Lean-feedback up to 8-16 times, and the authors equate it with Pass@64-256 of whole-proof sampling. One hard problem was proved with refinement but needed Pass@8192 without it. IMO 2025 statements were formalised by human experts at contest time.
numbers: Light setting n*m = Pass@8-16 times 8-16 refinements, 1-2 hours. IMO 2022 P2: solved with refinement, Pass@8192 without. PutnamBench: light 201/657, medium 331/657. MiniCTX-v2 (written after Nov 2024): 81.8% vs o4-mini 44.3% at Pass@8. miniF2F-test 99.6%. IMO 2025: 4/6 in time (5/6 after the deadline; P1 finished late). Heavy runs took days.
limits: Self-report, closed model, no ablation table for refinement vs Pass@k at matched tokens. Compute for heavy setting not given. Formal statements were checked by humans for IMO, but not audited elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Gives one same-lab claim that checker-guided refinement beats equal Pass@k. Also shows a clean uncontaminated test (MiniCTX-v2, after Nov 2024).

source: Ammanamanchi, Bhat, Biderman (2026) Faults in Our Formal Benchmarking (ICML 2026)
finding: First audit of Lean benchmark statements and harnesses. Kernel-checked does not mean correct: 398 mechanically certified issues (counterexamples, vacuous theorems, unsound axioms). A Lean bug let apply? accept a proof with a hidden sorry, and it hit three DeepSeek-Prover-V2 7B claimed proofs.
numbers: 13 benchmark variants, about 10,318 problems scanned (miniF2F 488, ProofNet 371, FormalMATH 5,560, CombiBench 100, ProverBench 325): 4,833 findings, 398 certified (text also says 399). apply? bug in Lean before 4.20.0: one miniF2F and two PutnamBench proofs claimed by DeepSeek-Prover-V2 7B. Test: 20 problems with proven issues, original statements unprovable, 0/20 solved by both models; after correction DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B solved 3/20 and Kimina-Prover-8B 2/20.
quote: The kernel only checks that a proof establishes a formal statement; it does not verify that the statement faithfully encodes the intended informal problem
limits: Counts are not deduplicated (forks, ports). Does not audit Seed-Prover or Hilbert outputs. Inflation size is shown only on small samples; no headline score recomputed.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 2: false verifications exist but are a handful of proofs in the open audit (3 flagged), not a measured percent of 2025 headlines. Our verifier must forbid axioms and sorry and use a second checker.

source: Ammanamanchi et al. (2026) Faults in Our Formal Benchmarking, LLM audit and direction of error
finding: Defects both inflate and deflate scores. Impossible items lower scores. Weakened statements (as in ProofNet vs ProofNet#) raise scores. LLM judges find nearly all bad statements but with many false alarms.
numbers: 92-problem labelled set, 552 classifications: Sonnet 4.5 + thinking precision 0.30, recall 0.82, F1 0.42, accuracy 68.1%, cost $13.71; GPT-5.2 + thinking precision 0.24, recall 0.91, F1 0.37, accuracy 54.6%, $6.86. ProverBench LLM filter cut findings 427 to 277 while keeping all confirmed true positives. Gemini 3.0 Flash 83.3% on a 55-example warning set.
limits: Challenge set is not a prevalence sample. Human review is final.
agent_relevance: If our agent judges its own formalisation, expect high recall and low precision: use it as a screen, not as a verdict.

source: Poiroux, Weiss, Kuncak, Bosselut (2024/2025) ProofNet# and BEq+ for statement autoformalization
finding: A direct check of flawed formal statements: 31.8% of two Lean 4 ports of ProofNet were wrong. Autoformalization of statements is still weak.
numbers: 118 of 371 entries (31.8%) had formalization errors. Best statement autoformalization 45.1% on ProofNet# (50 samples plus selection) vs 31.0% single generation. BEq+ pass@n on a validation split rose from 4.11% at n=1 to 40.54% at larger n. On long statements BEq+ falls to 29.6% from 62.5% on short ones. 3,752 annotated examples in ProofNetVerif.
limits: Statement fidelity metric. This is about ProofNet (Lean 4 ports), not the 2025 prover outputs.
agent_relevance: The upstream of every formal proof is an informal-to-formal step that fails often. A scaffold that restates a problem into a checkable form needs its own check of the statement.

source: Wang et al. (2025/ICLR 2026) Hilbert: recursively building formal proofs with informal reasoning
finding: Hilbert's depth ablation shows decomposition helps, but the baseline is a prover at pass@4 and the token spend is millions per problem, so it is not a matched comparison. The reasoner model matters hugely: gpt-oss-120b gets 13.3% on PutnamBench vs Gemini 2.5 Pro 70.0%.
numbers: miniF2F with Gemini 2.5 Pro plus Goedel-Prover-V2-32B: D=0 (no decomposition, prover pass@4) 75%, D=2 98.36%, D=3 98.7%. PutnamBench (660): Gemini 2.5 Pro variant 462/660 (70.0%); gpt-oss-120b variant 88/660 (13.3%). Avg tokens per solved problem: miniF2F 0.8-3.3M (Gemini variants), PutnamBench 24.4M; hardest problems 22.8M-27.0M tokens. Best config at most 4.5K reasoner and 11.3K total calls vs DeltaProver 16,384 calls.
limits: Different compute classes: D=0 spends about 4 samples, D=3 spends millions of tokens. No flat prompting at matched tokens. No output audit for false proofs reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: decomposition clearly helps, but the size at equal tokens is unmeasured. Reasoner strength dominates the gain.

source: Wang et al. (2025/ICLR 2026) Hilbert, retrieval ablation
finding: Adding a retriever of theorems helps pass rate a little and cuts compute a lot, mainly by stopping wrong theorem names.
numbers: miniF2F: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B variant 98.4% with retrieval vs 97.1% without; Goedel-V2-32B 99.2% vs 97.9%. Goedel variant: reasoner calls 862 to 548, reasoner tokens 4.0M to 2.3M, prover calls 449 to 391. DeepSeek variant: prover calls 290 to 205, reasoner tokens 2.1M to 1.9M.
limits: Retrieval is from Mathlib names (formal library), at ceiling pass rates. Averages are over samples needing decomposition.
agent_relevance: Supports K05: retrieval saves tokens even when accuracy is near ceiling.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Lyra: Orchestrating Dual Correction in Automated Theorem Proving
finding: A different group re-ran DSP with GPT-4 as the writer and got the same level as the Codex numbers, then added tool and error-message correction. With GPT-4 or human informal proofs, uncorrected DSP stays near 39-40% on miniF2F-test, and correction lifts it by 5-8 points at the same attempt count.
numbers: miniF2F-test, 100 attempts: Codex + human informal 39.3% (DSP original); Codex + 540B Minerva informal 38.9%; GPT-4 formal + GPT-4 informal 38.9% (valid 48.3%); GPT-4 + human informal 39.7% (valid 47.9%); with Tool Correction and Conjecture Correction GPT-4 informal 44.2% (valid 52.8%) and human informal 47.1% (valid 52.0%). At 200 attempts human informal 51.2% (valid 55.3%); GPT-4 informal 47.9%/54.9%. Subgoal-Learning 45.5%.
limits: Not an independent replication in the strict sense (builds on DSP, same Isabelle pipeline, same miniF2F). GPT-4 is a 2023 drafter; no 2025 reasoning model drafter was tested. Tool Correction uses Sledgehammer, which only exists in Isabelle.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 4: DSP's 39% holds with another formal model and a weaker drafter (GPT-4 informal 38.9 = Minerva 38.9). Whether stronger drafters help is mixed; Hilbert (d11) shows the reasoner strength matters a lot.

source: Thakur et al. (2024) COPRA: in-context learning agent for formal theorem proving (COLM 2024)
finding: A stateful loop with execution feedback beats the same number of independent samples. Informal proofs add only a little on top of retrieval.
numbers: miniF2F-test with GPT-4: few-shot 1 sample 13.52%; few-shot 60 samples (T=0.7) 15.98%; COPRA 60 queries 26.63%; without backtracking 24.59%; plus retrieval 29.09%; plus retrieval and informal proofs 29.92%; 100 queries 30.74%. ReProver 25.00%. Few-shot GPT-3.5 2.8%, COPRA GPT-3.5 9.02%.
limits: Equal number of queries, but COPRA prompts carry history and each query returns one tactic, so tokens per query differ. COPRA runs retrieval and informal runs only on problems still unsolved. Informal-proof gain (+0.83) is small and measured on one run, no confidence interval.
agent_relevance: Best same-domain equal-query evidence for K04: feedback loop +10.65 points over 60 independent samples. Informal proof adds 0.8 on top (K07 weak).

source: Lu, Delaware, Zhang (2024) PALM: Proof Automation with Large Language Models (ASE 2024)
finding: A manual error taxonomy of GPT-3.5 Coq failures, and a fix-by-category ablation. Most failing categories can be repaired by mechanical rules; the biggest part of the gain is backtracking.
numbers: 520 GPT-3.5 errors on Verdi: wrong theorem application 258 (49.6%), invalid reference 79 (15.2%), incorrect rewrite 61 (11.7%), redundant introductions 56 (10.8%), tactic misuse 44 (8.5%), bullet misuse 19 (3.7%), misc 3 (0.6%). On 10,842 CoqGym theorems: PALM 4377 (40.4%); each repair mechanism removed leaves 37.8-39.2% (PALM wins by 3.0-6.9%); without backtracking 702 (6.5%), so backtracking adds 523.5% (5x); every variant proves 65.2-71.5% more than DSP.
limits: Taxonomy by two coders (first author labelled, second author reviewed; 52 person-hours); one model (GPT-3.5) and one language (Coq). First error only. The scaffold uses a Coq-specific symbolic repair tool.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 mostly closed: top error is applying the wrong theorem (half). Backtracking and premise retrieval are scaffold-only fixes. Rewrite, reference and bullet errors are fixable by rules and are small share.

source: Thompson et al. (2025) Rango: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Proving for Automated Software Verification (ICSE 2025)
finding: Retrieving similar earlier proofs (not just lemmas) is the main gain. The advantage over other tools shrinks on projects after the training cutoff.
numbers: CoqStoq benchmark (10,396 theorems): Rango 32.0%, 29% more than Tactician, 66% more than Proverbot. Ablation, 500 theorems: full 160 (32.0%); without lemma retriever 159 (31.8%); without proof retriever 111 (22.2%); without retrieval 89 (17.8%). Rango proves 47% more than the no-proof-retriever variant. File-wise split (leaky): full 36.8%, no retrieval 25.4%. Post-cutoff projects (1,171 theorems): Rango 352 (30.1%), Tactician 331 (28.3%), Proverbot 217 (18.5%).
limits: Retrieval from the same project's earlier proofs. Fine-tuned model. Post-cutoff edge over Tactician is only 1.8 points of 1,171.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: retrieving similar solved cases is the single largest lever in-domain (+10 points). Transfer to non-formal tasks is not tested.

source: Wang et al. (2023/ICLR 2024) LEGO-Prover: growing library of verified lemmas
finding: A library of lemmas proved earlier in the same run helps later proofs. Ablation removing it costs about 3 points.
numbers: miniF2F-valid, 50 attempts, ChatGPT: with skill library 50.4%, without 47.1% (+3.3). Main result 100 attempts: valid 57.0%, test 50.0%; over 20,000 skills added (22,532 in library).
limits: Ablation only on miniF2F-valid and only at 50 attempts due to cost. Single run. The gain is verified-lemma reuse; it needs a checker to certify skills.
agent_relevance: Closest analog of memory of solved sub-problems: only verified items go in. For our agent, store only checker-passed items.

source: Gulati et al. (2025) Putnam-AXIOM: functional and static benchmark
finding: Contamination signal on informal Putnam problems: the same problems with changed constants score much lower. This is a text-answer benchmark, not Lean, but it applies to PutnamBench-era problems.
numbers: 522 original problems and 100 variations. o1-preview 219/522 = 41.94% on the original set and 19.6 points lower (46.8% relative) on variations; 18 other models fall too, 10 with non-overlapping 95% CIs. Drops reported: DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-32B 37.5%, GPT-4o 36%, o1-preview 17% (a smaller measure on a matched subset).
limits: Informal answers, not formal proofs. Drop can also reflect variants being harder. Not run on Lean provers.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: contamination for Putnam problems is likely real for general LLMs. For formal provers no equivalent variant test has been found.

source: Jain et al. (2025) What's in a Proof? Expert proof-writing processes in F* and Verus
finding: Telemetry and screen recordings of eight experts show a plan-first, few-open-errors style succeeds more. A small F* agent built on these rules did better than o4-mini with the same prompt. No LLM-copilot user study found in this search.
numbers: N=8 experts (4 F*, 4 Verus), 4 tasks, about 90-minute sessions, task time 11.8-45 minutes. F* clusters: Planners (shortest median time, 100% success), Rapid Verifiers (7.3 verifier calls per min, slower and less successful). Experts with 0-4 active errors did better than those with more than 15. Baseline o4-mini could not solve the selected tasks in 30 verifier loops; agent needed fewer calls (authors say 3.75x fewer).
limits: Eight people, small tasks, no novices, no LLM in the human loop. Agent comparison is a small case study, unspecified seeds.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for LLM-copilot user studies. This gives scaffold rules: draft the spec first, split into subgoals, keep few open errors, check often but not blindly.

source: Lean community reports via search (2026): Collatz 'disproof' from kernel bug; Zulip on Prover-V2 misformalisation
finding: Search snippets (not read in full) say a Lean kernel bug in nested inductive projections briefly let a false Collatz claim pass in July 2026, and a Zulip maintainer said one DeepSeek-Prover paper proof was for a misformalised miniF2F theorem.
numbers: No counts in snippet. One kernel bug, patched in about an hour per the snippet; the second checker Nanoda also accepted it per the snippet.
limits: Snippet only; claims not verified by opening the pages. Treat as lead, not evidence.
agent_relevance: A single-kernel verdict can be wrong: add a second independent check for high-stakes S8 passes. Marked unopened.
